 It’s turkey, Black Friday, and football. Not in that order. New Wednesday and Friday games are part of a strategy for year-round domination.
 Print this Article 
 View Comments Photo Illustration by Ally Rzesa/Globe Staff; Adobe Peter King wrote for Sports Illustrated from 1989 to 2018, and has been named National Sportswriter of the Year three times. His new book is “ The Game .” 
 Remember when Thanksgiving meant two NFL games? It was a Detroit Lions game, a Dallas Cowboys game, and that was it. 
 This year, for the first time, the Thanksgiving slate starts Wednesday evening on Netflix. There will be three more games on Thanksgiving itself, followed by a Black Friday game on Amazon. Almost a third of the league will kick off before Sunday. 
 No sport dominates the calendar like this. And it won’t stop. Last week, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones suggested an 18th regular season game could begin as early as next season . 
 Two visionary commissioners made this happen. Paul Tagliabue and Roger Goodell are top-­20 figures in the history of the game, in no small part because they put football front of mind for sports fans 11 months a year. Today, football never sleeps. It just naps for three or four early-summer weeks.

Enter Email Sign Up Before Goodell and Tagliabue supercharged the calendar, an earlier commissioner, Pete Rozelle, thought absence made the heart grow fonder, and the disappearance of pro football for five-­plus months made fans want it more come August. 
 Back in the 1980s, the offseason was an off season. No televised scouting combine, no free agency, no pro days, no draft overkill, no wall-­to-­wall spring minicamp coverage, no Back to Football weekend at the end of July, no grandiose Hall of Fame weekend in August. Nothing really, except a one-­day draft in the spring, starting at eight in the morning in a New York hotel ballroom with only the first round and a half broadcast on TV. If you wanted to know who your team drafted, you had to check the agate type in the newspaper the next morning. 
 By the turn of the century, free agency and the NFL Scouting Combine were becoming the Next Big Things. Draft guru Mel Kiper Jr. was a bigger football name in springtime than superstars Montana and Rice and Marino. But draft overkill wasn’t enough. The NFL was entering its Gordon Gekko period. Greed — ­football greed — ­was good. Year-­round football talk grew in the Tagliabue years, 1989 to 2006, and it would become a way of life when Goodell took over as commissioner. 
 Now, when network executives and on-­air talent meet with league officials for their annual preseason briefings on the new year, part of the presentation is the NFL calendar wheel — ­an invention, in 2009, of league marketing and events staffers. Here is the 2026 calendar wheel: It’s 14 months, from January 2026 to February 2027, with four quadrants: The Future (the combine and draft), Back to Football, The Season, Postseason. The climax of the calendar, at 12 o’clock, is Super Bowl LXI in Inglewood, Calif. Look at the thing. It’s chock-­full — ­but maybe, for Goodell, not full enough. 
 Imagine it as a clock face. Look at about 3:30. See the minicamp logo for May/June, and the NFL Flag Championships logo, for ESPN’s live coverage of the youth flag football championships, July 17-­20? There’s an inactive month there; minicamps are over by June 15 or 20 every year, and NFL teams take three to four weeks off when spring practices end. Next are the flag games in Canton, Ohio, a month later. 
 The commissioner is not satisfied with the month-­long hiatus. He wants his events and marketing teams to find something big for late June. By the time you read this, the calendar could have another event. Something, perhaps, like the NFL’s version of Comic-­Con or Fanatics Fest, a four-­day weekend of fantasy football, player meet-­and-­greets, catching a pass from an NFL quarterback, panels of players on issues of the day, panels of coaches on trends, panels of NFL legends, autograph sessions, etc., at a huge convention center or even stadium, perhaps in a relatively central location. Imagine an event for thousands of fans, or maybe tens of thousands — ­say, at Jerry Jones’s AT&T Stadium outside Dallas — ­on the last long weekend of June. 
 “Roger has a restless dissatisfaction with the status quo,” said the man he has charged with filling the calendar wheel, Peter O’Reilly, the league’s executive vice president for club business, international and league events. “That Back to Football quadrant, there’s such a strong desire to be doing more in that space. How do we ensure we’re serving our fans year-­round, with a set of partners who are all in on that?” 
 The NFL has developed a crazy ethos along the lines of “If you build it, they will come.” If it has something to do with pro football and you put it out in the media, someone will pay attention. Enter Steve Bornstein, who proved it. 
 The keystone in the year-­round calendar, I believe, was NFL Network. History has shown the TV network to be an underachiever. It never became the power player that every cable and satellite provider hoped it would be. But it was an impact player in one way: It forced the league to expand its horizons, sometimes nonsensically, to give the fledgling network programming beyond a few live games and some studio shows and the best the NFL Films vault had to offer. NFL Network invented some things no right-­minded person would consider good TV . . . and, to a degree, led the rest of the media covering the league to expand their coverage, too. 
 Bornstein, a vaunted TV executive, became the first NFL Network boss at its founding in 2003. He had the presidencies of ESPN and ABC on his résumé. 
 “When I first came in, I’m looking at everything. I needed content in May, when no one was thinking about the NFL. I thought we could do a schedule-­release show. I totally understood the pushback: ‘Wanna watch grass grow? Watch the schedule-­release show!’ But we knew what we did at the network would force ESPN to eventually pay more attention to this kind of programming, and this was about creating events that would prompt the media to focus more on our off­season than they ever had.” 
 Think about the annual late-­April/early-­May release of the schedule. When the last regular-­season game of the previous year is done in January, all 32 teams know every foe they’ll be facing in the fall. The schedule simply puts dates to the games and determines the national TV schedules for all the networks. That’s it. It matters to three groups, really: to the teams, for road-­trip-­planning purposes; to networks, who find out if they got all the big games they wanted; and to ardent fans, who care about their team’s opening day foe or might follow their teams to a road game or two. Otherwise, who on earth cares if the Falcons play the Niners on Sept. 14 or Dec. 14? 
 Tagliabue chose to make it a TV show, though a sparsely watched one. At first. By 2022, NFL Network had 22 reporters/hosts, some at team facilities, covering the three-hour release of the schedule, and ESPN even began two-­hour prime-time specials competing with NFL Network’s show. 
 In addition, ESPN expanded its popular weekday “NFL Live” show from in-­season to 52 weeks a year, boosting the NFL’s off­season profile in a big way. Rich Eisen, the on-­air face of NFL Network at its 2003 birth, said the goal was to fill “the 30 weeks in which everyone misses the other 22.” 
 I understood back in the day Pete Rozelle feeling like less is more, but that was in a different time in this country. I just watched “E.T.” with my kids, and there’s that scene with the phone, the landline on the wall. I stopped the movie and said to them, “See that thing hanging on the wall with the cord? It’s a phone.” Now you cannot hibernate for six or seven months. You cannot cede the field of play anymore. 
 Jaime Weston was the first manager of a new NFL department, Brand and Creative, established by the league in 2003. She said the emphasis on year-­round programming was about giving fans what they wanted — ­and about serving women. 
 “We listened to fans and gave them what they wanted.” she said. “Take the draft. The draft used to be a bunch of big fans, men, jammed into Radio City in midtown Manhattan. Now, at the draft, you see lots of women and families. Forty-­eight percent of NFL fans are women, and women want to be treated like real fans. Don’t just make a pink jersey and shrink it down to fit me; serve me. Why does the draft work on the weekend, after the first round? People don’t come together a whole lot anymore in person. But they come together for the draft. You don’t need a season ticket. It’s not expensive. Families, strollers, lots of kids.” 
 Talking to Weston, I found myself thinking of Mark Cuban, the maverick former principal owner of the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks. In 2014, Cuban railed against the NFL expanding its TV package to Thursday nights, saying the league already owned prime time on Sundays and Mondays, and football’s greed would end up backfiring. Cuban told reporters: “I think the NFL is 10 years away from an implosion. I’m just telling you: Pigs get fat, hogs get slaughtered. And they’re getting hoggy. Just watch . . . when you’ve got a good thing and you get greedy, it always, always, always, always, always turns on you. That’s rule No. 1 of business.” 
 Let’s see how Cuban’s words have aged. 
 In 2014, the average NFL game was watched by 17.7 million TV viewers. That rose to 18.7 million in 2025. The Super Bowl audience was 7 million viewers higher in 2024 than a decade earlier. 
 The NFL was at the beginning of a new TV contract in 2014, and three years into one in 2024. Average TV rights fees earned by the league in each season: $5.5 billion in 2014, $10.1 billion in 2024. A doubling. 
 Per Forbes, the average NFL franchise value was $1.43 billion in 2014 — ­and $6.49 billion in 2024. An increase of 354 percent in 10 years. 
 A few months before Cuban spoke, in late 2013, the Gallup organization asked Americans, “What is your favorite sport to watch?” Football got 39 percent of the vote; basketball and baseball, second and third on the list, combined for 26 percent. Same poll in 2023: Football 41 percent, basketball/baseball, 19 percent. Big gain for football. 
 “I think the NFL is 10 years away from an implosion.” Maybe Cuban meant explosion. The NFL owns the American sporting landscape, this Thanksgiving week, for sure, but not just in the autumn. Even the haters see that today.
